text: In a recorded lecture, S-rank summoner Park Doyun put seven perfectly coordinated constructs through their paces. They felt no pain and no fear. Send them in, and nobody else had to go.
At 2:46 a.m., Taeo was still watching. He hadn't felt Nib once during the tunnel survey, and he couldn't stop thinking about it.
From under his blanket, Nib told him to turn off the shouting brick. Taeo asked for one more lecture.
If a construct seems to want something, Doyun said, question your own desires. Nib had no trouble naming his. 'I want sleep.'
The next morning, Nib asked about the missing porter. No update. The company still said he had left voluntarily.
Voluntarily meant by choice, Taeo explained. So who saw him leave, Nib asked. The report named no one.
Nib had pressed the tunnel wall, just like at the store. Taeo had felt nothing. Nib told him to find out why.
At the yard, the mule kept walking into plywood. One command at a time, Taeo suggested. Stop, its summoner said. It stopped.
Haein recognised Doyun's influence at once. Taeo had watched all twelve lectures. It showed on his face.
He tried the lecture's focused attention technique on Nib. Nothing. 'I'm not in lecture four,' Nib said.
Taeo told Haein how the pulse vanished. Did it fade, or cut out? He had been too scared to notice. So she proposed measuring it.

Minho arrived, having just turned down a C-grade job at its offered rate. He gave them an hour with the training gate. Radios could report positions, but they couldn't warn him when a scout's support slipped.
The little licensed gate had a snail for a boss. Minho's rule: nobody steps on it. Killing it would close the gate and cost them their licence.
The test: three identical beams holding sandbags. Nib would secretly pull one pin and test each beam. Blindfolded outside, Taeo had to name the one that slipped. Three runs.
The blindfold was a sock. Clean, Haein promised. Mostly.
Nib's terms: no guessing. If Taeo felt nothing, he said nothing. Taeo agreed.
Nib crossed, and the amber glow faded from Taeo's palm again.
Under a green sky, Nib pulled the middle beam's pin. The snail kept eating lichen.
Outside, amber pressure flickered back into Taeo's hand. One beam at a time. The first held.
Nib leaned on the middle beam. Its foot slid, and Taeo felt the pressure drag sideways across his palm. Beam two.
Nib came out raising two fingers. First call, correct.
On the second run, Taeo felt nothing. The seconds dragged. Pressed for a call, he offered a hesitant two.
Nib came out holding up one finger. Taeo had guessed. Don't apologise to the data, Haein said. Nib asked to go again.
Third run. Taeo breathed slowly. No guessing. This time he clearly felt the first two beams hold.
Holding on took effort. A thin line of blood ran from his nose before he noticed.
Inside, the third beam kicked out. Nib caught the falling plank on his shoulder and stopped a tumbling sandbag with his foot, just short of the snail.
Pressure slammed across Taeo's palm, then vanished. He shouted for Nib, leapt off the crate, and charged over the chalk line, still blindfolded.
Minho caught him just short of the rim and held him there.
Nib came out unhurt and raised three fingers. Taeo pulled off the sock, grinning. Two out of three.
Then Haein pointed at his nose. Taeo touched his lip, saw the blood, and lost the grin.
Nib tilted his head forward and handed him a napkin. Was it the link? Taeo didn't know. Nib approved of that answer.
The snail survived. Minho's newest white hair went to Taeo.
That afternoon, Bluebird came to repossess one of the family's three vans. The towing fee, two hundred and twenty thousand won, went on their debt.
Haein rescued her father's field notebooks first. Bluebird wasn't taking those.
It had been Dongsik's first van. Nib's hand drifted toward his knife. Taeo stopped him. Let them take it, Minho said. They owed the money.
The truck left an empty space between the remaining vans. Nib stood in it, watching the road.
By evening, Minho had taken the Guro job. He had refused it that morning, Haein reminded him. 'That was this morning.'
Thursday: a C-grade gate in a Guro construction pit, with porters from Dokgo Contracting. Taeo recognised the name. The missing porter's company.
Minho already knew. The decision hadn't come easily.
He offered Nib the scouting job, and Nib accepted at once. Then Minho turned to Taeo. Stay outside.
He always stayed outside, Taeo said.
Minho pointed at the sneaker prints crossing the broken chalk line. 'You stay outside.'
